newsitem.title: USA: Strong winds may have flattened weak US corn crop.
newsitem.headline: Strong winds may have flattened weak US corn crop.

text.p: Strong winds were blowing across key U.S. corn growing areas on Wednesday, posing a threat to crops whose stalks were already weakened by widespread problems with corn borers, meteorologists said.

"When you take into account there is a lot of corn still to harvest and weakened stalks because of corn borer these type of winds should lead to significant problems with crop lodging," Joel Burgio of Weather Services Corp said.
Strong winds of up to 63 miles per hour were reported in the northwest Corn Belt, with the most powerful in the leading corn growing state, Iowa, he added.
Burgio of WSC said the winds were already in northern Illinois, Iowa and Minnesota and would move east into northern Indiana and Michigan during the day.

Winds reached 63 miles per hour (mph) in Burlington, in southeast Iowa and 61 mph in Sioux City in the northwest part of the state. Des Moines in central Iowa had reports of up to 58 mph winds and Waterloo in the northeast, 55 mph.
Iowa's corn crop was 35 percent harvested, as of Sunday, well behind the five-year average pace of 56 percent, according to weekly data issued by the Iowa Agricultural Statistics Service.
Tim Bowden, meteorologist with Weather Express, said winds started to pick up in Nebraska during mid-afternoon Tuesday, reaching 40 mph with gusts up to 55 mph.
"They were a little bit stronger in Iowa. We don't normally see winds like this except for winter storms," Bowden, who is based in Omaha, Neb., said.

He said the system brought cold air funnels (shortlived minor tornadoes) to the Minneapolis area and rainfall of 1.00 to 1.50 inches to South Dakota, southern Minnesota, Wisconsin, northeast Iowa and the extreme northwest of Illinois. Eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa had 0.25 to 0.50 inches.
